idiom_name: proxy + activation queue + scheduler thread + future
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form of the six roles: give the object a proxy that turns each method call into a Method Request (arguments plus a result slot) and appends it to a bounded Activation Queue; run one scheduler loop in a private thread that dequeues runnable requests and invokes call() on the Servant; return a Future to the caller for every two-way method. The Servant is owned by the scheduler thread, so it needs no locks and must never be touched from outside. Express run-time ordering constraints as request guards and terminate the scheduler with an explicit shutdown protocol rather than by killing the thread.
code_sketch:
proxy.put(msg):
    req = MethodRequest(call=servant.put_i, args=(msg,), future=Future())
    activation_queue.enqueue(req)
    return req.future

scheduler_thread():
    loop:
        req = activation_queue.dequeue_runnable()  # waits until a queued guard is true
        result = req.call()                        # executes on the servant
        req.future.set_result(result)              # completion phase
pitfalls: Wrong move: call the servant directly from the proxy -> the client thread mutates servant state and bypasses queue ordering; instead enqueue a Method Request and let the Scheduler invoke the servant.

Wrong move: leave the activation queue unbounded -> when arrivals exceed service capacity, latency and memory grow without bound; instead bound it and choose whether producers block, requests are rejected, or work is shed.

Wrong move: block the servant on another request or its own Future -> the single scheduler thread waits for work that it alone can execute, causing self-deadlock; instead compose asynchronously or call a different active object.

Outstanding futures left un-awaited when the object shuts down: callers that never call get() silently lose their result or exception, so shutdown must complete all pending futures exceptionally and callers must be documented to observe them.

Cyclic channel topologies with bounded channels: actor A sending to a bounded channel to actor B while B sends to a bounded channel to A deadlocks when both channels fill; keep channel topology as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), or use oneshot channels / try_send for request-response legs to break the cycle.

Holding a lock across an await/suspend point: when the servant calls an async operation, any lock it holds is held for the entire suspension duration, allowing other tasks to observe inconsistent state or causing priority inversion; move blocking work to spawn_blocking or a dedicated worker thread.

Natural actor shutdown via channel-close detection: when all senders to an mpsc channel are dropped, recv() returns None — exploit this for zero-message shutdown protocols rather than explicit stop messages for simple actors.

Unbounded queues for high-volume data-plane traffic: acceptable for low-frequency control-plane messages but dangerous for data-plane workloads where producers can outpace consumers indefinitely; always use bounded channels and define overflow policy (block, drop, shed).
